title: Image and likeness
hook: Orthodox teachers say we have God's image and grow into his likeness

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation and evolution: one page, read as plain days or as a pattern. Your line was god of all time. What old thing did you stop and look at? Day one thousand seventy-five.

"And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." That's Genesis, in the King James Bible, on the sixth day. Read it fast and it sounds like one idea said twice. Image, likeness: same thing, surely? Some readers take it that way. But some early Christian teachers slowed right down on that pair. Two words, they said, two gifts. One you're born with. One you grow into. That reading lives on in the Orthodox churches of the East, and it changes how a whole life looks. Today: image and likeness.
screen: `LET US MAKE MAN IN OUR IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the image. In this reading, the image of God is given, whole, to every human being. Genesis says it plainly in the very next verse: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Nobody earns it. Nobody loses it. A baby has it. A prisoner has it. The person who annoys you most has it. Orthodox teachers speak of it as something like the stamp of the maker, and they point to the mind and freedom that make a person a person. Then the likeness. That's not a stamp; it's a resemblance. It's what happens when the image starts to show in how someone actually lives: when patience, mercy and love grow in them, slowly, like a child growing to look like a parent. In Orthodox teaching, that growing is the whole Christian life, and it goes all the way: they call it theosis, becoming by grace like God. Paul has a line that sounds like this kind of growth. In the King James: "we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory." From glory to glory. Not in one leap. Other Christians read image and likeness as one idea said twice, and they talk about growth with other words: sanctification, becoming holy. The shape is close. But the two-word reading gives a memorable picture: a gift that's already yours, and a face you grow into. The image is given. The likeness is grown.

Here's the practice: grow a little into likeness today. Settle, and breathe. First, think of one person you find hard to be around. Hold them in mind for a moment, and remember: in this teaching, they carry the image too, whole. Then think of one quality you'd like to see grow in you. Patience. Gentleness. Honesty. Courage. Just one. Picture one small moment later today when it could show. If you pray, you can ask for help to grow toward it. If you don't, just hold the picture of that moment, clearly, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Image and likeness. In Orthodox teaching, the image of God is given to every person; the likeness is grown into, slowly, by grace.
Your line: image given, likeness grown. Today, let the one quality you picked show once, even in a small way, even if nobody notices. Day one thousand seventy-five.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians speak of growing from the image into the likeness of God, a lifelong path they call theosis, walked through prayer, the sacraments and love of neighbor; other churches speak of the same growth as sanctification.

original.note: Hebrew: image. The first of the two words in Genesis 1:26; the second, likeness, is demut.

trapdoor: what you thought: image and likeness, two words for the same thing.
what it means: in Orthodox teaching, the image is given to every person, and the likeness is grown into over a lifetime.
what a scholar hears: some read the pair as one idea said twice; Orthodox teachers read a starting gift and a goal, theosis.

notes: The image/likeness distinction is credited to 'some early Christian teachers' (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.6 and 5.16; John of Damascus, Exposition 2.12, image as mind and free will, likeness as likeness in virtue). Confirm references.
'Hebrew writing can say a thing twice for weight' (parallelism) is a general claim; confirm or cut.
'Nobody loses it' states the Orthodox position that the image is not lost through sin; some Western teachers speak of the image as damaged or defaced. Confirm the phrasing is fair for the broad path.
Original: צֶלֶם (tselem), image; demut, likeness. Confirm vocalization and stress.
Theosis is introduced briefly; it may be taught more fully later in year four.

Editor: the KJV verse has no 'and' between image and likeness ('in our image, after our likeness'), so 'that little word and' became 'that pair'; cut the unsourced claim about Hebrew saying things twice (hook and trapdoor); 'reason, mind and freedom' trimmed; garbled screen head replaced.
Auditor (year-4 pass): read in full; quotations checked against the KJV, attributions and framing checked; no changes needed.
